decks.title: Admission of a Partner — Part 1: Ratios and Goodwill
goals: Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio in every type of admission
Account for goodwill under Accounting Standard 26: premium in cash or kind, partly or not brought, old goodwill written off
Calculate hidden goodwill from capital contributions and pass the entry

slides.heading: Admission of a Partner
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **new profit-sharing ratio**, the **sacrificing ratio** and **goodwill** on admission. All firms and figures in this chapter are imagined.

nodes.label: Admission and its adjustments
New ratio
Sacrificing ratio
Goodwill (premium)
Hidden goodwill

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what changes on admission, the new profit-sharing ratio, the sacrificing ratio, goodwill brought as premium, and hidden goodwill
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A growing firm often needs fresh money, new skills or a bigger network, so it admits a new partner. The newcomer buys a share in the assets and a share in the future profits. In this first part we work out how profits will now be shared, who gives up what, and how the old partners are paid for the goodwill they built.

slides.heading: What changes when a partner joins
bullets: Admission creates a **new agreement**: the old firm is reconstituted.
The new partner gets the right to a **share in assets** and a **share in future profits**.
Before he joins, six matters are settled (see the flow).

nodes.label: New profit-sharing ratio
Sacrificing ratio
Goodwill
Revaluation of assets and liabilities
Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
Capitals and the new balance sheet

visual.alt: Flow of the six adjustments made on admission: new profit-sharing ratio, sacrificing ratio, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits or losses, and capitals with the new balance sheet
visual.caption: Six matters to settle on admission

slides.narration: Admission ends the old agreement and starts a new one, so the books must be put in order first. We fix the new profit-sharing ratio and the sacrificing ratio, treat goodwill, revalue assets and liabilities, distribute reserves and past profits or losses, and finally settle the capitals and draw up the new balance sheet. This part covers the first three.

slides.heading: Where does the new partner's share come from?

headers: How the new partner gets his share
New share of each old partner
rows: From all old partners in the old ratio
Each surrenders a fraction **of his own share**
Each gives a fraction **of the firm**
Whole new share from him; others nil

visual.alt: Table of the ways a new partner can get his share: from all old partners in the old ratio, by each surrendering a fraction of his own share, by each giving a fraction of the firm, from one partner only, or with the new ratio given; for each it shows how to find the sacrifice and the new share
visual.caption: Sacrifice = old share − new share in every case.

slides.narration: The newcomer's share always comes out of the old partners' shares, but the terms can differ. All old partners may give in their old ratio, each may surrender a fraction of his own share, each may give a fraction of the whole firm, one partner may give it all, or the new ratio may simply be stated. In every case, sacrifice equals old share minus new share.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: share taken in the old ratio
slides.body_md: Saffron Prints, Nashik (imagined): Neha and Omkar share **3 : 2**. Pallavi joins for **1/5**, taken from both in their old ratio.
bullets: Step 1 — Each old partner keeps 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 of his or her share.
Step 2 — Multiply, then write all shares over one denominator.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: Neha's share 3/5 becomes 12/25, Omkar's 2/5 becomes 8/25 and Pallavi gets 5/25, so the new ratio is 12 : 8 : 5 and the sacrificing ratio is 3 : 2
visual.caption: Sacrificing ratio = old ratio 3 : 2.

slides.narration: Pallavi takes one fifth, so the old partners keep four fifths of their own shares. Neha's three fifths times four fifths is twelve twenty-fifths. Omkar's two fifths times four fifths is eight twenty-fifths. Pallavi's one fifth is five twenty-fifths. The new ratio is twelve to eight to five, and because both gave in the old ratio, the sacrificing ratio is still three to two.

slides.heading: Quick check: one partner gives the whole share
slides.body_md: Only the giving partner's share falls.
slides.narration: Subtract the new partner's share from the one partner who gives it, and leave the other share untouched.

slides.heading: Old and new shares, side by side
slides.body_md: The new partner's slice is cut out of the old slices.

visual.caption: Old and new profit shares, worked example 1.

slides.narration: Each bar stands for the whole profit of the firm. In the old firm, Neha has three fifths and Omkar two fifths. In the new firm, Pallavi's slice is cut out of both, in the ratio three to two, so Neha drops to twelve twenty-fifths and Omkar to eight twenty-fifths. The bars are the same length, because the shares always add up to one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: partners surrender parts of their own shares
slides.body_md: Brahmaputra Tea Traders, Guwahati (imagined): Arjun and Bela share **5 : 3**. Charu joins; Arjun surrenders **1/5 of his share** and Bela **1/3 of hers**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: Arjun gives up 1/5 of 5/8, that is 1/8; Bela gives up 1/3 of 3/8, also 1/8; Charu gets 1/4; the new ratio is 2 : 1 : 1 and the sacrificing ratio 1 : 1, although the old ratio was 5 : 3

slides.narration: Arjun surrenders one fifth of five eighths, which is one eighth. Bela surrenders one third of three eighths, also one eighth. Charu therefore gets one fourth. Arjun is left with one half and Bela with one fourth, so the new ratio is two to one to one. Notice that the sacrificing ratio is one to one, not the old five to three.

slides.heading: Quick check: the sacrificing ratio formula
slides.body_md: Complete the formula.
slides.narration: A sacrifice is what a partner gives up. Which share do you subtract from the old share?

slides.heading: Goodwill on admission and Accounting Standard 26
bullets: **Premium for goodwill** = firm's goodwill × new partner's share.
Only **purchased goodwill** can be recorded, so goodwill is **not raised** in the books on admission.

nodes.label: Old partners give up part of future profits
New partner compensates them: premium for goodwill
Credited in the sacrificing ratio
No goodwill account raised (Accounting Standard 26)

visual.alt: Flow: the old partners give up part of their future profits; the new partner compensates them with a premium for goodwill; it is credited to them in the sacrificing ratio; no goodwill account is raised because Accounting Standard 26 allows only purchased goodwill
visual.caption: Why a premium is paid

slides.narration: The old partners built the firm's reputation, and now they give up part of the profits it will earn. So the new partner pays them a premium for goodwill, equal to the firm's goodwill times his share. Accounting Standard twenty-six allows only purchased goodwill to be recorded, so no goodwill account is opened. The premium simply passes to the sacrificing partners.

slides.heading: Goodwill entries in each situation

rows: Bank A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
Asset A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c and To new partner's Capital A/c
New partner's Capital (or Current) A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c
No entry in the firm's books

visual.alt: Table of goodwill entries on admission: premium in cash goes through the premium for goodwill account to the sacrificing partners; premium in kind debits the asset; premium not brought debits the new partner's capital or current account; withdrawal debits old capitals and credits bank; a private payment needs no entry

slides.narration: Here are the situations you will meet. Premium in cash goes through the premium for goodwill account to the sacrificing partners. Premium in kind debits the asset brought. If the newcomer cannot pay, his capital or current account is debited instead. If the old partners withdraw the premium, their capitals are debited and the bank credited. A private payment needs no entry.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: premium brought in cash
slides.body_md: Saffron Prints: goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. Pallavi (1/5) brings ₹80,000 as capital and her premium in cash.

rows: *(Capital and premium brought in cash by Pallavi)*
*(Premium credited to the sacrificing partners in 3 : 2)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example 3: bank debited 1,10,000 rupees, crediting Pallavi's capital 80,000 and premium for goodwill 30,000; then premium for goodwill debited and Neha credited 18,000 and Omkar 12,000

slides.narration: Pallavi's premium is one fifth of rupees one lakh fifty thousand, that is rupees thirty thousand. The bank receives her capital and premium together. The premium account is then closed by crediting the sacrificing partners in three to two: Neha gets rupees eighteen thousand and Omkar rupees twelve thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: premium partly brought
slides.body_md: Brahmaputra Tea Traders: goodwill is valued at ₹96,000. Charu (1/4) brings only ₹10,000 of her premium.

rows: *(Part of the premium brought in cash by Charu)*
*(Goodwill credited to the sacrificing partners; the unpaid part charged to Charu)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example 4: bank debited 10,000 rupees for the premium brought; then premium for goodwill 10,000 and Charu's capital 14,000 debited, crediting Arjun and Bela 12,000 rupees each

slides.narration: Charu's full premium is one quarter of rupees ninety-six thousand, which is rupees twenty-four thousand. She brings only rupees ten thousand. The old partners must still receive the full amount in their sacrificing ratio of one to one, rupees twelve thousand each, so the unpaid rupees fourteen thousand is debited to Charu's capital account in the same entry.

slides.heading: Quick check: premium not brought
slides.body_md: Who is debited, and who is credited?
slides.narration: The newcomer still owes the compensation. Which account carries that charge?

slides.heading: Goodwill already in the books, and withdrawals
bullets: Old goodwill is written off **before** the new arrangement, in the **old ratio**.
A withdrawal of premium leaves the firm with less cash and the old partners with smaller capitals.

rows: Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c
Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c

visual.alt: Table: goodwill already in the books is written off by debiting the old partners in the old ratio; premium withdrawn by the old partners is debited to their capital accounts and credited to bank

slides.narration: Sometimes the old balance sheet already shows goodwill. It belongs to the old firm, so it is written off among the old partners in their old ratio before anything else. And if the old partners take the premium out of the business, we debit their capital accounts and credit the bank.

slides.heading: Hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: When no premium is mentioned, the new partner's **capital** can reveal the firm's goodwill.

nodes.label: New partner's capital ÷ his share = implied total capital
minus (old partners' adjusted capitals + new partner's capital) = hidden goodwill
Hidden goodwill × new partner's share = his premium
Debit his capital (or current) account; credit sacrificing partners

visual.alt: Flow for hidden goodwill: divide the new partner's capital by his share to get the implied total capital, subtract the actual capitals to get hidden goodwill, multiply by his share for his premium, and debit his capital account crediting the sacrificing partners
visual.caption: Hidden goodwill, step by step

slides.narration: Sometimes nothing is said about goodwill, but the new partner agrees to bring a capital that is large for his share. Divide his capital by his share to get the total capital the firm is worth to him. Subtract the capitals actually in the new firm. The difference is hidden goodwill. His share of it is debited to his capital and credited to the sacrificing partners.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Ganga Agencies, Varanasi (imagined): Ishaan and Jaya share **3 : 1**; capitals after adjustments ₹90,000 and ₹50,000. Kabir joins for **1/4** with ₹60,000, no premium.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 5: implied capital 2,40,000, actual capital 2,00,000, hidden goodwill 40,000, Kabir's share 10,000 credited to Ishaan 7,500 and Jaya 2,500 rupees
visual.caption: Entry: Kabir's Capital A/c Dr. ₹10,000 To Ishaan's Capital A/c ₹7,500 and Jaya's Capital A/c ₹2,500.

slides.narration: Kabir's rupees sixty thousand for one quarter values the capital at rupees two lakh forty thousand. The capitals actually in the firm are rupees ninety thousand plus rupees fifty thousand plus his own rupees sixty thousand, a total of rupees two lakh. So hidden goodwill is rupees forty thousand, and Kabir's quarter, rupees ten thousand, is debited to him and credited to Ishaan and Jaya in three to one.

slides.heading: Quick check: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Implied capital, minus actual capital, times the new share.
slides.narration: Follow the three steps on the flow and give your answer in rupees.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Old share − new share, for each old partner
Sacrificing partners, in the sacrificing ratio
Debit new partner's capital or current account
Write off in the old ratio

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: new share in the old-ratio case, sacrificing ratio as old minus new, premium as goodwill times the new share, credited to sacrificing partners, debit to the new partner if not brought, old goodwill written off in the old ratio, and hidden goodwill from the capitals

slides.narration: To sum up: the new partner's share comes out of the old partners' shares, and each sacrifice is old share minus new share. The premium for goodwill equals the firm's goodwill times the new share and goes to the sacrificing partners. If it is not brought, the newcomer's capital is charged. Old goodwill is written off in the old ratio, and hidden goodwill is read from the capitals.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always **show the sacrificing ratio** before passing goodwill entries; do not assume it equals the old ratio.
Read the wording: a fraction **of his share** is multiplied; a fraction **of the firm** is subtracted directly.
Check that the new shares **add up to one**.
Write a short **narration** under every journal entry; partial marks depend on it.
Never open a **goodwill account** for the premium or for hidden goodwill.
slides.narration: A few exam habits will save marks. Work out the sacrificing ratio explicitly, because it is often not the old ratio. Read carefully whether a partner gives a fraction of his own share or of the whole firm. Check that all new shares add up to one. Write a narration under each entry, and never raise a goodwill account on admission.

decks.title: Admission of a Partner — Part 2: Revaluation, Reserves, Capitals and the New Balance Sheet
goals: Prepare the revaluation account and share its result among the old partners
Distribute reserves and accumulated profits or losses on admission
Adjust capitals on the basis of the new partner's capital (or find his capital from the old capitals) and prepare the new balance sheet

slides.heading: Revaluation, reserves and the new balance sheet
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **revaluation**, **reserves**, the **capital accounts**, adjusting **capitals** and the **new balance sheet**.

nodes.label: Revaluation
Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
Capital accounts
Adjusting capitals
New balance sheet

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits or losses, partners' capital accounts, adjustment of capitals, and the new balance sheet
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In the first part we settled ratios and goodwill. Now we bring the books up to date before the new partner steps in. We revalue assets and liabilities, hand out reserves and past profits or losses to the old partners, adjust the capitals, and finish with the balance sheet of the new firm, all with one imagined spice firm from Kochi.

slides.heading: Why revalue before admission?
bullets: Book values may be **out of date**: buildings rise, stock loses value, liabilities are missed.
Gains and losses up to admission belong to the **old partners**, in the **old ratio**.

nodes.label: Book values are out of date
Revalue assets, reassess liabilities
Gain or loss belongs to the old firm
Shared by old partners in the old ratio

visual.alt: Flow: book values are out of date, so assets are revalued and liabilities reassessed; the gain or loss belongs to the old firm and is shared by the old partners in the old ratio
visual.caption: Why revalue before admission

slides.narration: Books show assets at historical figures, which may be far from their real worth on the day of admission. A building may have risen in value, some stock may be damaged, and an expense may be unpaid. If we ignore these, the new partner would share gains or losses that arose before he joined. So we revalue first and give the result to the old partners.

slides.heading: The revaluation account
columns:
**Debit (losses)**

- Fall in an asset
- Rise in a liability
- Unrecorded liability
- New provision

**Credit (gains)**

- Rise in an asset
- Fall in a liability
- Unrecorded asset
- Provision released

rows: Decrease in the value of an asset
Increase in the value of an asset
New or higher provision (e.g. for doubtful debts)
Balance: profit to old partners (old ratio)
Balance: loss to old partners (old ratio)

visual.alt: Table of the revaluation account format: the debit side has decreases in assets, increases in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities and new provisions, with a profit balance to the old partners; the credit side has increases in assets, decreases in liabilities and unrecorded assets, with a loss balance to the old partners
visual.caption: Also called the profit and loss adjustment account.

slides.narration: The revaluation account works like a small profit and loss account. Anything that reduces the firm's net worth goes on the debit side: a fall in an asset, a rise in a liability, an unrecorded liability, or a new provision. Anything that increases it goes on the credit side. The balance is a profit or a loss for the old partners in their old ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: revaluation account
slides.body_md: Nilgiri Spices, Kochi (imagined): Rohan and Simran share **2 : 1**. On Tara's admission: stock falls by ₹6,000; building rises by ₹30,000; a 5% provision is made on debtors of ₹40,000; rent of ₹1,000 is outstanding; ₹3,000 of creditors will not be claimed.

rows: Profit transferred to Rohan's Capital A/c
Profit transferred to Simran's Capital A/c

visual.alt: Revaluation account of Nilgiri Spices: losses on stock 6,000, provision 2,000 and outstanding rent 1,000; gains on building 30,000 and creditors 3,000; profit 24,000 rupees shared Rohan 16,000 and Simran 8,000

slides.narration: Put the losses on the debit side: stock six thousand, the provision two thousand and the rent one thousand. Put the gains on the credit side: building thirty thousand and creditors three thousand. The credit side is bigger by rupees twenty-four thousand, a profit. Rohan takes two thirds, rupees sixteen thousand, and Simran one third, rupees eight thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: who shares the revaluation profit?
slides.body_md: Think about when the change in value happened.
slides.narration: Did the change in value happen before or after the new partner joined?

slides.heading: Reserves and accumulated profits or losses

headers: Item in the old balance sheet
rows: General reserve; credit balance of profit and loss
Debit balance of profit and loss; deferred revenue expenditure
Claim first; balance credited (an excess claim is a revaluation loss)
Fall in investments first; balance credited (an excess fall is a revaluation loss)

visual.alt: Table of reserves on admission: general reserve and credit profit and loss are credited to old partners in the old ratio; accumulated losses are debited; workmen compensation reserve first meets the claim and investment fluctuation reserve first meets the fall in investments, with balances credited

slides.narration: Reserves and undistributed profits were earned by the old partners, so they are credited to them in the old ratio. Accumulated losses, such as a debit balance in profit and loss, are debited to them the same way. Special reserves first do their own job: workmen compensation reserve meets the claim, and investment fluctuation reserve meets the fall in investments. Only the balance is shared.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: reserves at admission
slides.body_md: Tapti Textiles, Surat (imagined): Uday and Vani share **3 : 2**. At Wasim's admission: general reserve ₹40,000; debit balance of profit and loss ₹10,000; workmen compensation reserve ₹15,000 against a claim of ₹9,000.

rows: *(General reserve transferred to the old partners in 3 : 2)*
*(Accumulated loss written off among the old partners)*
*(Claim provided out of the reserve; balance to the old partners)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example 7: general reserve 40,000 credited Uday 24,000 and Vani 16,000; accumulated loss 10,000 debited 6,000 and 4,000; workmen compensation reserve 15,000 meets a claim of 9,000 with the balance 6,000 credited 3 : 2

slides.narration: The general reserve of rupees forty thousand is credited three to two, rupees twenty-four thousand and rupees sixteen thousand. The accumulated loss of rupees ten thousand is debited the same way. The workmen compensation reserve first covers the claim of rupees nine thousand, and only the balance of rupees six thousand goes to Uday and Vani.

slides.heading: Quick check: an accumulated loss
slides.body_md: A debit balance of profit and loss is a past loss.
slides.narration: Whose loss is it, and in which ratio is it shared?

slides.heading: The partners' capital accounts
slides.body_md: Prepare them in **columnar form**, one column per partner, including the new partner.

nodes.label: Old balances b/d
+ revaluation profit, reserves, premium (old partners)
− revaluation loss, accumulated losses, old goodwill written off
+ capital brought by the new partner
± surplus or deficit if capitals are adjusted
Balance c/d → new balance sheet

visual.alt: Flow of entries in the partners' capital accounts: opening balances, plus revaluation profit, reserves and premium for old partners, minus losses and old goodwill, plus the new partner's capital, plus or minus capital adjustments, and the closing balances carried to the new balance sheet
visual.caption: Order of entries in the capital accounts

slides.narration: All these adjustments meet in the partners' capital accounts, kept in columnar form. Start with the opening balances. Credit the old partners with revaluation profit, reserves and premium; debit them with losses and old goodwill. Credit the new partner with the capital he brings. Any capital adjustment comes last, and the closing balances go to the new balance sheet.

slides.heading: Adjusting old partners' capitals
bullets: **Total capital** = new partner's capital ÷ his share.
**Required capital** of an old partner = total capital × his new share.
Surplus: withdrawn in cash or credited to his **current account**; deficit: brought in cash or debited to his current account.

nodes.label: New partner's capital ÷ his share = total capital
Total × each old partner's new share = required capital
Compare with adjusted capital
Surplus: withdraw or credit current account; deficit: bring cash or debit current account

visual.alt: Flow for adjusting old partners' capitals: divide the new partner's capital by his share for the total capital, multiply by each old partner's new share for his required capital, compare with his adjusted capital, then settle the surplus or deficit in cash or through current accounts
visual.caption: Capitals in the new ratio

slides.narration: Partners often agree that capitals should be in the new profit-sharing ratio. Take the new partner's capital as the base and divide it by his share to get the total capital. Multiply by each old partner's new share to find what he should have. Compare this with his adjusted capital, then settle the surplus or the shortage in cash or through current accounts.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: capitals made proportionate
slides.body_md: Kosi Electricals, Patna (imagined): Yash and Zoya share equally. Amaan joins for **1/5** (old ratio) with ₹50,000. Adjusted capitals: Yash ₹1,12,000, Zoya ₹91,000. Differences are settled in cash.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 8: total capital 2,50,000; Yash and Zoya each need 1,00,000; Yash has 1,12,000 and withdraws 12,000; Zoya has 91,000 and brings 9,000 rupees
visual.caption: Total capital = ₹50,000 ÷ 1/5 = ₹2,50,000.

slides.narration: Amaan's rupees fifty thousand for one fifth means a total capital of rupees two lakh fifty thousand. The new ratio is two to two to one, so Yash and Zoya each need two fifths, rupees one lakh. Yash has rupees twelve thousand too much and withdraws it; Zoya is rupees nine thousand short and brings it in.

slides.heading: Quick check: total capital
slides.body_md: Start from the new partner's capital and his share.
slides.narration: Divide the new partner's capital by his share of profit.

slides.heading: Or: the new partner's capital from the old capitals
slides.body_md: Sometimes the **old partners' capitals** are the base and the **new partner's capital** is the unknown.

rows: Their combined share in the new firm

visual.alt: Table: old partners' adjusted capitals of 1,80,000 rupees stand for three quarters of the new firm, so total capital is 2,40,000 and the new partner's one-quarter capital is 60,000 rupees

slides.narration: Sometimes it works the other way round. The old partners' adjusted capitals are taken as the base. Together they hold three quarters of the new firm, so rupees one lakh eighty thousand stands for three quarters, and the whole capital is rupees two lakh forty thousand. The new partner, with one quarter, brings rupees sixty thousand. Always finish every adjustment to the old capitals first.

sections.heading: 1. Admission and the adjustments it needs
sections.body_md:
A new partner may be admitted with the consent of all existing partners (unless the deed says otherwise). Admission **reconstitutes** the firm: the old agreement ends and a new one begins. The new partner acquires two rights: a **share in the assets** and a **share in the future profits** of the firm.

**Matters to settle on admission**
1. New profit-sharing ratio.
2. Sacrificing ratio.
3. Goodwill (premium, or adjustment through capitals).
4. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities.
5. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses.
6. Capitals (and, if agreed, their adjustment) and the new balance sheet.

key_terms.definition_md: Entry of a new partner into an existing firm, which reconstitutes the firm.
A change in the agreement among partners while the firm continues.

sections.heading: 2. New profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio
sections.body_md:
**Sacrifice of an old partner = old share − new share.** The sacrificing ratio is the ratio of these sacrifices.

| Terms of admission | How to compute |
|---|---|
| Share taken in the old ratio | New share = old share × (1 − new partner's share); sacrificing ratio = old ratio |
| Fraction **of his own share** surrendered | Sacrifice = old share × fraction |
| Fraction **of the firm** given | Sacrifice = that fraction |
| One partner gives the whole share | Only his share falls |
| New ratio given | Sacrifice = old − new for each |

Always check that the new shares add up to 1, and that the sacrifices add up to the new partner's share.

sections.heading: 3. Goodwill on admission (Accounting Standard 26)
sections.body_md:
**Premium for goodwill = firm's goodwill × new partner's share.** It is credited to the **sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio**. Accounting Standard 26 allows only purchased goodwill to be recorded, so **no goodwill account** is raised on admission.

- **In cash:** Bank A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c; Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs.
- **In kind:** Asset A/c Dr. To Premium for Goodwill A/c and To new partner's Capital A/c.
- **Partly or not brought:** New partner's Capital (or Current) A/c Dr. (unpaid part) To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs.
- **Withdrawn by old partners:** Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank A/c.
- **Paid privately:** no entry.
- **Goodwill already in the books:** written off in the **old ratio** — Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c.

sections.heading: 4. Hidden goodwill
sections.body_md:
When no premium is stated but the new partner brings a capital that is high for his share:

1. **Implied total capital** = new partner's capital ÷ his share.
2. **Actual capital** = old partners' capitals **after all adjustments** + new partner's capital.
3. **Hidden goodwill** = implied − actual.
4. **New partner's share** = hidden goodwill × his share: New partner's Capital (or Current) A/c Dr. To sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs.

sections.heading: 5. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
sections.body_md:
A **revaluation account** (profit and loss adjustment account) records changes in values at admission.

- **Debit:** decrease in assets, increase in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities, new provisions.
- **Credit:** increase in assets, decrease in liabilities, unrecorded assets, provisions no longer needed.
- **Balance:** profit (credit to old partners) or loss (debit to old partners) in the **old ratio**.

Typical entries: Revaluation A/c Dr. To Stock A/c (fall); Building A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c (rise); Revaluation A/c Dr. To Old partners' Capital A/cs (profit).

sections.heading: 6. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
sections.body_md:
Reserves and accumulated profits belong to the old partners and are shared in the **old ratio**:

- **General reserve / credit balance of profit and loss:** Reserve A/c Dr. To Old partners' Capital A/cs.
- **Debit balance of profit and loss, deferred revenue expenditure (e.g. advertisement suspense):** Old partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To the account.
- **Workmen compensation reserve:** meets the claim first; the balance is credited to old partners; an excess claim is debited to revaluation.
- **Investment fluctuation reserve:** meets the fall in investments first; the balance is credited to old partners; an excess fall is debited to revaluation.

key_terms.definition_md: Profits earned before admission and kept in the business as reserves or as a credit balance.
Reserve kept for claims of workers for injury; on admission it first meets any claim.

sections.heading: 7. Capitals and the new balance sheet
sections.body_md:
**Capital accounts** are prepared in columnar form for all partners; closing balances go to the new balance sheet.

**Old partners' capitals on the basis of the new partner's capital**
- Total capital = new partner's capital ÷ his share.
- Required capital of each old partner = total capital × his new share.
- Surplus → withdrawn (Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c) or credited to his current account; deficit → brought in (Bank A/c Dr. To Capital A/c) or debited to his current account.

**New partner's capital on the basis of the old partners' capitals**
- Total capital = old partners' adjusted capitals ÷ their combined new share; new partner's capital = total capital × his share.

**New balance sheet:** assets and liabilities at revised values, unrecorded items added, reserves removed, closing capitals (and any current accounts) shown.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Crediting the premium in the **old ratio** when the sacrificing ratio is different.
- Multiplying when a partner gives a fraction **of the firm**, or subtracting when he surrenders a fraction **of his own share**.
- Giving the new partner a share of revaluation profit or reserves.
- Opening a goodwill account for premium or hidden goodwill.
- Comparing capitals before **all** adjustments (revaluation, reserves, premium) are made.
- Forgetting to add the new partner's cash (capital and premium) to the bank in the new balance sheet.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 3 marks: a ratio calculation with steps, or two or three journal entries with narrations.
- 4 marks: entries for two cases, or a revaluation account with capital accounts.
- 6 marks: revaluation account (about 2), capital accounts (about 2), new balance sheet (about 2); working notes earn step marks.

questions.stem_md: When a person is admitted into an existing firm as a new partner, he or she normally acquires two rights. These are the right to

options.text_md: a fixed salary and interest on capital
a share in the assets and a share in the future profits of the firm
manage the firm alone and sign all its contracts
withdraw the reserves built up by the old partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a share in the assets and a share in the future profits of the firm. A new partner buys into the property of the firm and into its future profits. Salary and interest depend on the deed, and sole management or a claim on old reserves is not a right of admission.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 24 : 18 : 7. Each old partner keeps 6/7 of his or her share: Hema 4/7 × 6/7 = 24/49, Iqbal 3/7 × 6/7 = 18/49, and Jatin 1/7 = 7/49.

old share × new share

questions.stem_md: A new partner takes his share of profit from the old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio. In this case the sacrificing ratio of the old partners is

options.text_md: always equal among the old partners
the same as their new ratio
the same as their old ratio
the same as their capital ratio

answer.model_answer_md:

Any goodwill amount the partners agree on in the deed

questions.stem_md: Explain why a new partner is asked to bring a premium for goodwill, and state how it is dealt with in the books when (i) it is brought in cash and (ii) it is not brought at all.
questions.solution_md: Link the premium to the sacrifice of future profit; in both cases the credit goes to the sacrificing partners, only the debit changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Why:** the old partners built the reputation and customer base of the firm and give up part of their future profits to the newcomer, who will share in profits that this goodwill helps to earn. The premium compensates them for that sacrifice.

**(i) Brought in cash:** Bank A/c is debited and Premium for Goodwill A/c credited; the premium account is then closed by crediting the sacrificing partners' capital accounts in the sacrificing ratio.

**(ii) Not brought:** the new partner's capital (or current) account is debited with his share of goodwill and the sacrificing partners' capital accounts are credited. No goodwill account is opened, as Accounting Standard 26 recognises only purchased goodwill.

questions.stem_md: Assets and liabilities of a firm are revalued at the time of admitting a partner so that

options.text_md: the new partner neither gains nor loses from changes in value that took place before he joined
the new partner bears a share of all past losses
the firm can pay less income tax in the year of admission
the old partners can withdraw their capitals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the new partner neither gains nor loses from changes in value that took place before he joined. Changes in value belong to the period of the old firm; recording them before admission keeps the newcomer out of past gains and losses.

questions.stem_md: The account opened on admission to record increases and decreases in the values of assets and liabilities is called the ___ account.
questions.solution_md: It is the revaluation account (also called the profit and loss adjustment account).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is debited to the revaluation account on the admission of a partner?

options.text_md: An increase in the value of land
An unrecorded liability now brought into the books
A decrease in the amount payable to creditors
An unrecorded investment now brought into the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An unrecorded liability now brought into the books. A newly recorded liability reduces the firm's worth, which is a loss on revaluation. Rises in assets, falls in liabilities and newly found assets are gains, credited to the account.

questions.stem_md: Profit or loss on revaluation at the time of a partner's admission is shared by

options.text_md: all the partners, including the new one, in the new ratio
the old partners in their sacrificing ratio
the new partner alone
the old partners in their old ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the old partners in their old ratio. The change in values took place before the newcomer joined, so it belongs to the old partners in the ratio in which they shared profits then.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm's balance sheet shows a workmen compensation reserve of ₹20,000. On a partner's admission, a claim for workmen compensation of ₹26,000 is established. The correct treatment is

options.text_md: the reserve is used up and the excess claim of ₹6,000 is debited to the revaluation account
the whole reserve of ₹20,000 is credited to the old partners in the old ratio
₹6,000 is credited to the revaluation account
the claim is ignored because a reserve already exists

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the reserve is used up and the excess claim of ₹6,000 is debited to the revaluation account. The reserve covers 20,000 of the claim; the remaining 6,000 is an extra liability, a loss for the old partners through revaluation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm has an investment fluctuation reserve of ₹12,000. Its investments, shown at ₹80,000, have a market value of ₹74,000 when a new partner is admitted. The treatment of the reserve is

options.text_md: ₹12,000 is credited to the old partners in the old ratio
₹6,000 is debited to the revaluation account
₹6,000 is credited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
₹12,000 is debited to the revaluation account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹6,000 is credited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. The fall of 6,000 is met from the reserve; the balance 12,000 − 6,000 = 6,000 is a past profit of the old partners.

questions.stem_md: At the time of admission, the balance sheet of an imagined firm shows a debit balance in the profit and loss account. This balance is

options.text_md: credited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
debited to all the partners in the new ratio
debited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
carried forward to the balance sheet of the new firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. A debit balance is a loss of the period before admission, so the old partners bear it in their old ratio.

questions.stem_md: On the admission of a partner into an imagined flour mill at Ujjain, land is revalued up by ₹45,000 and machinery down by ₹8,000; a provision for doubtful debts of 5% is created on debtors of ₹60,000; an electricity bill of ₹2,000 is outstanding but unrecorded; and creditors of ₹1,500 will not be claimed. options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Revaluation records changes in value that happened while the old partners ran the firm, so only they share it, in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: A general reserve in the books at the time of admission is transferred to the capital accounts of the ___ partners in their ___ ratio.
questions.solution_md: The reserve is a past profit, so it goes to the old partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: Match each item found on a partner's admission with its treatment.

options.text_md: Increase in the value of a building

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md:
Dinesh, Elina and Faraz are partners in Damodar Steel Traders, an imagined steel stockist at Dhanbad, sharing profits 2 : 2 : 1. Their balance sheet as at 31 March 2026 was:

| Liabilities | ₹ | Assets | ₹ |
| --- | --: | --- | --: |
| Creditors | 60,000 | Bank | 35,000 |
| General Reserve | 30,000 | Debtors | 65,000 |
| Dinesh's Capital | 1,00,000 | Stock | 70,000 |
| Elina's Capital | 1,40,000 | Patents | 10,000 |
| Faraz's Capital | 30,000 | Plant | 1,80,000 |
| **Total** | **3,60,000** | **Total** | **3,60,000** |

On 1 April 2026 they admit Garima for 1/5 share: she gets 1/10 of the firm's profit from Dinesh and 1/10 from Faraz, while Elina's share does not change. (a) Garima brings ₹80,000 as capital and her share of goodwill in cash; goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. (b) Patents are worthless and stock is to be increased by ₹5,000. (c) The old partners' capitals are to be made proportionate to the new ratio on the basis of Garima's capital, by opening current accounts.

Prepare the revaluation account, the partners' capital accounts and the balance sheet of the new firm.
questions.solution_md: Only Dinesh and Faraz sacrifice, so only they receive the premium; current accounts absorb every difference, so no cash moves for the adjustment.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Working notes**

1. New shares: Dinesh 2/5 − 1/10 = 3/10; Elina 2/5 − 0 = 2/5; Faraz 1/5 − 1/10 = 1/10; Garima 1/10 + 1/10 = 1/5.
2. New ratio (Dinesh : Elina : Faraz : Garima) = **3 : 4 : 1 : 2**; sacrificing ratio (Dinesh : Elina : Faraz) = **1 : 0 : 1**.
3. Revaluation: gains ₹5,000 − losses ₹10,000 = loss ₹5,000, shared in the old ratio 2 : 2 : 1 (Dinesh ₹2,000, Elina ₹2,000, Faraz ₹1,000).
4. General Reserve ₹30,000 is credited to the old partners in the old ratio 2 : 2 : 1 (Dinesh ₹12,000, Elina ₹12,000, Faraz ₹6,000).
5. Premium for goodwill = ₹1,50,000 × 1/5 = **₹30,000**, credited to the sacrificing partners in 1 : 0 : 1.
6. Brought in cash: Dinesh ₹15,000, Faraz ₹15,000.
7. Total capital on the basis of Garima's capital = ₹80,000 ÷ 1/5 = ₹4,00,000.
8. Dinesh: required ₹4,00,000 × 3/10 = ₹1,20,000; adjusted capital ₹1,25,000; surplus ₹5,000 credited to the current account.
9. Elina: required ₹4,00,000 × 2/5 = ₹1,60,000; adjusted capital ₹1,50,000; deficit ₹10,000 debited to the current account.
10. Faraz: required ₹4,00,000 × 1/10 = ₹40,000; adjusted capital ₹50,000; surplus ₹10,000 credited to the current account.
11. Bank: ₹35,000 (opening) + ₹80,000 (Garima's capital) + ₹30,000 (premium) = ₹1,45,000.
